blocks.text: Fine-tuning is the process of taking a model that has already been trained on a broad, general dataset and continuing its training on a smaller, focused dataset so it becomes better at a specific task or adopts a specific style.

Rather than teaching a model everything from the very first weight, fine-tuning starts from a model that already understands language, code, or images in general, and nudges that existing understanding toward the exact job you actually need done.
1. What Fine-Tuning Actually Means

blocks.alt: A pretrained model goes through additional training to become a specialized model

blocks.text: At its core, fine-tuning is just more training. You take the numerical weights of a model that already exist, and you run a smaller, targeted training process on top of them using data that reflects the task you care about.
The word tuning is deliberate. You are not building an instrument from raw materials, you are adjusting one that already plays, so that it plays the specific piece you need.

blocks.title: Not a separate technology
blocks.content: Fine-tuning is not a different kind of model or a different architecture, it is a training procedure applied to an existing set of weights.

blocks.text: 2. From General Purpose to Specialized

blocks.alt: A general purpose model is compared against a task specialized model

blocks.text: A general purpose model, the kind released by a lab after pretraining, has seen an enormous and varied slice of text, code, or images, and as a result it can hold a reasonable conversation about almost anything.

That breadth is also its limitation. A general model tends to be average at many things rather than excellent at one thing, and it may not know your internal terminology, your preferred tone, or the exact output format your application expects.

Fine-tuning trades some of that breadth for depth in one direction. After fine-tuning, the model still remembers most of what it knew before, but its behavior shifts noticeably toward the examples it was just shown.
3. Starting From Pretrained Weights

blocks.alt: Pretrained weights serve as the starting point that gets further adjusted

blocks.text: Every fine-tuning run begins by loading a checkpoint, a saved snapshot of every weight in the network, produced by an earlier and far larger pretraining run.

Those weights already encode grammar, facts, coding patterns, and reasoning ability. Fine-tuning does not discard any of that, it continues adjusting the same weights using a new, narrower set of examples.

blocks.text: 4. What Actually Changes During Fine-Tuning

blocks.alt: Example inputs move through a forward pass into a weight update

blocks.text: During fine-tuning, each training example is fed through the model, the model produces a prediction, that prediction is compared against the correct answer, and the weights are nudged slightly to make a similar prediction more likely next time.
This is the same basic mechanism used during pretraining, gradient descent adjusting weights to reduce a loss value, just applied for a much shorter run on a much smaller, more focused dataset.

blocks.title: Small nudges, not a rebuild
blocks.content: A single fine-tuning run typically changes weights by a tiny fraction of their original values. The model is nudged, not rebuilt.

blocks.text: 5. A Concrete Example: A Generic Model Learns Your Support Tone

blocks.alt: A generic model is fine-tuned on support ticket examples to produce a support-toned model

blocks.text: Suppose you run a customer support team and you want an assistant that replies in your company voice, always opens with an apology when appropriate, and always closes with a specific sign-off.

A general purpose model can write a reasonable support reply, but it will not consistently match your voice unless you either describe that voice in detail every single time, or you fine-tune the model on hundreds of real, edited replies your team has already sent.
After fine-tuning on those examples, the model tends to produce replies in that same voice by default, without needing the instructions repeated in every request.
6. Fine-Tuning Is Training, Just Starting From a Head Start

blocks.alt: Training from scratch is compared against fine-tuning, which starts with a head start

blocks.text: Training a model completely from scratch means starting every weight at a random value and teaching it language itself, a process that costs enormous amounts of compute and data.

Fine-tuning skips that entire phase. It begins from weights that already understand language, so the amount of data and compute needed is dramatically smaller, often a difference of many orders of magnitude.
7. The Fine-Tuning Loop at a Glance

blocks.alt: Loading pretrained weights, feeding examples, updating weights, and saving the fine-tuned model

blocks.text: A fine-tuning run follows a simple loop: load the pretrained weights, feed the model a batch of task specific examples, measure how wrong its predictions were, update the weights slightly, and repeat this many times over the dataset.
Once the loop finishes, the adjusted weights are saved as a new checkpoint, a fine-tuned model that behaves like the original but shifted toward the new data.

code.content:
# A simplified sketch of the fine-tuning loop
for batch in training_data:
    predictions = model(batch.inputs)
    loss = compute_loss(predictions, batch.targets)
    loss.backward()
    optimizer.step()
    optimizer.zero_grad()

save_checkpoint(model, "fine-tuned-model")

blocks.text: 8. What You Need to Fine-Tune a Model
A fine-tuning project needs three ingredients, a pretrained base model to start from, a dataset of examples that show the behavior you want, and enough compute to run the training loop for a while.
The exact amount of each ingredient varies enormously depending on the model size and the fine-tuning method chosen, a topic covered in later modules of this course.

items: A base model, chosen for its size and its existing capability in the relevant domain
A dataset, ranging from a few dozen curated examples to millions of records
Compute, ranging from a single consumer GPU to a large multi-node cluster
A way to evaluate whether the fine-tuned model actually improved on the task

blocks.text: 9. Full Fine-Tuning vs Efficient Fine-Tuning, A First Look

The earliest form of fine-tuning updates every single weight in the model, known as full fine-tuning. It gives the most flexibility but requires storing gradients and optimizer state for the entire model, which is expensive for large models.

A newer family of methods, parameter efficient fine-tuning, updates only a small added set of parameters while leaving the original weights frozen. This course covers both approaches in depth, full fine-tuning first, then parameter efficient methods like LoRA.

blocks.text: 10. Common Misconceptions About Fine-Tuning

Fine-tuning is sometimes assumed to be the answer to every model limitation, but it does not add new factual knowledge reliably, it does not replace the need for good prompts, and it does not guarantee better performance if the training data is poor.

blocks.title: Fine-tuning shapes behavior, not facts
blocks.content: Fine-tuning is best understood as shaping how a model responds, its tone, format, and task alignment, rather than as a way to teach it new facts on demand.

blocks.text: 11. Where Fine-Tuning Fits in the Model Lifecycle
A typical large language model lifecycle moves through pretraining, then optional fine-tuning stages, then alignment training, then deployment and monitoring in production.

Fine-tuning usually sits after a team has already tried prompting and retrieval based approaches and found them insufficient for the level of consistency or specialization the task demands, a decision this course returns to directly in a later topic.
Worked Example

A team building a legal document assistant starts with a general purpose language model. Using only prompts, the model produces reasonable summaries but frequently uses casual language inappropriate for legal documents and sometimes omits required disclaimers.

The team collects two thousand examples of properly formatted legal summaries written by paralegals, each paired with the source document. They fine-tune the general model on this dataset for a few epochs.

The resulting fine-tuned model now defaults to formal language and consistently includes the required disclaimer, without needing those instructions repeated in every prompt, because that behavior has been baked into the weights themselves through fine-tuning.
Common Mistakes

items: Assuming fine-tuning is always the right tool, without first trying prompting or retrieval, which are often cheaper and faster to iterate on
Fine-tuning on a tiny, low quality dataset and expecting large improvements
Treating fine-tuning as a way to add new facts, when it mostly reshapes style and task behavior
Skipping evaluation and assuming the fine-tuned model is better simply because training loss went down

blocks.text: Practice

Pick a task you are familiar with, such as writing product descriptions or answering support questions. Write down what a general purpose model does wrong on that task today, then decide whether the fix is really a fine-tuning problem or a prompting problem.
Key Takeaway

Fine-tuning continues training an already pretrained model on a smaller, focused dataset so its behavior shifts toward a specific task or style, trading some general breadth for reliable, repeatable specialization.
